query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high‐temperature BCC state, the phase stability upon cooling is governed by the magnitude of the thermodynamic driving force (ΔG between the BCC and competing fcc phase), which in turn controls the kinetic barrier for phase transformation. A larger ΔG (i.e. more destabilized BCC) should lead to more rapid and complete transformation to the fcc (or mixed) phase during controlled cooling or aging.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in a homogeneous high‐temperature BCC state.
generation.intervention: Execute a series of controlled heat treatments (e.g., isothermal holds during cooling) on samples that are kept at identical baseline conditions as well as on samples with minor compositional tweaks (e.g., slightly increased Co content) designed to modify ΔG_bcc-fcc.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in an inert atmosphere with identical cooling rates. Comparison between the baseline composition and tweaked compositions under the same thermal profile, particularly in the temperature regime where atomic diffusion becomes active (below the critical transformation temperature).
generation.structural_mediator: The evolving phase fractions (tracked by XRD, EBSD, and TEM) serve as a mediator linking the thermodynamic driving force to observable microstructural change.
generation.mechanism: A higher Gibbs free energy difference (ΔG_bcc-fcc) in the BCC phase (caused by minor compositional tuning) decreases its stability and reduces the kinetic energy barrier, thereby accelerating nucleation and growth of the more thermodynamically stable fcc phase upon cooling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with an enhanced ΔG (through a slight increase in Co or another destabilizing element) will exhibit faster and more complete transformation from BCC to fcc phases during controlled heat treatments compared to the baseline Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy.
generation.baseline: The baseline Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy subjected to the same cooling/aging treatment is expected to transform at a moderate rate, serving as a point of comparison.
generation.boundary: These predictions hold under conditions where diffusion is active (moderate to low temperatures during the hold) and in inert atmospheres; the effect may be obscured if extrinsic factors such as oxidation or severe compositional heterogeneity intervene.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative link between ΔG and transformation kinetics is supported by CALPHAD-based design and previous experimental observations, the precise quantitative relationship and the critical ΔG threshold for rapid transformation remain uncertain due to interplay with local compositional fluctuations and diffusion barriers.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) baseline Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 and (2) samples with a minor increase in Co to deliberately heighten ΔG_bcc-fcc. Subject both sets to identical heat treatment schedules involving isothermal holds in the critical temperature range. Monitor the evolution of phase fractions over time using XRD and EBSD.
measurements: Phase fraction of BCC versus fcc over time
Kinetic rates of transformation measured by time-resolved XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified samples (with increased ΔG) do not show a statistically significant acceleration in the transformation rate (i.e. a faster and more complete transition from BCC to fcc) compared to the baseline samples under the same conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Alloy design based on CALPHAD approach
cited_evidence.text: Alloying elements such as Fe, Cr, and V are considered firstly in the present MEA design. Fe is a cost-effective element in fcc MEA systems, and its increase helps to generate the formation of bcc or hcp phase. We set the Fe content to be 45 at.%, based on alloy-design conditions underlying that complex concentrated alloys (CCA) such as HEA and MEA are not Fe-based alloys but multi-principal-element alloys. Cr which improves the corrosion resistance is set to be 10 at.%. The third candidate element is 10 at.% of V. V is usually utilized in bcc refractory HEA fields, but can also be added to single-fcc-phase HEAs if the formation of sigma phase is suppressed. V possesses a larger negative mixing enthalpy and a resultantly stronger bonding with Fe, Co, and Ni than bonding between Cr, Fe, Co, and Ni. A substantial solid-solution hardening effect can also be expected by a high lattice distortion because the atomic size of V is considerably larger than that of Cr, Fe, Co, and Ni. In order to obtain a single fcc phase, thus, careful element control through a thermodynamic approach is primarily required.

The above results reveal that our design approach based on the difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases (ΔGbcc-fcc) can realize the fcc to bcc transformation in MEA research areas. The fraction of bcc and consequent transformation rate according to the Co content and temperature also well correspond to the thermodynamic phase stability. In this section, we discuss the microstructural evolution and phase stability, varied with the balance of Co and Ni, and their contributions to the mechanical response in detail.
